lead: The family of Jacob goes down into Egypt. At Beer-sheba, on the edge of the promised land, the old patriarch is afraid, and God speaks to him in the night: “Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt … I myself will go down with you.” In the Gospel Jesus sends the Twelve out “like sheep into the midst of wolves”, and promises that the Spirit of their Father will speak through them. Both readings are about being sent into a place that is not safe, with God going along. Psalm 37 gives the quiet confidence: the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, their refuge in time of trouble. Some places keep today the optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the martyrs of China; the readings are those of the weekday.

r.h: I will go down with you to Egypt
set: Joseph has revealed himself and Pharaoh has invited Jacob’s whole household to come and live in Egypt (45:16–20). Jacob, now called Israel, sets out with all that he has. In this chapter the text moves between his two names: Jacob, the name he was born with, and Israel, the name given after the struggle at the Jabbok (32:28).

Background. Beer-sheba is the southernmost place of the promised land, where Abraham planted a tree and called on the name of the Lord, and Isaac built an altar (21:33; 26:25). To go further is to leave the land God promised. Isaac had been told not to go down to Egypt in a famine (26:2), so Jacob’s hesitation is understandable. The words of God in v. 3 answer his fear. The reading leaves out the list of the seventy persons of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt (46:8–27).
str: vv. 1–4: at Beer-sheba Israel offers sacrifices, and God speaks in the night: do not be afraid; I will go down with you and bring you up again.
vv. 5–7: Jacob’s sons carry him, their families and their livestock into Egypt in Pharaoh’s wagons.
vv. 28–30: Judah leads the way to Goshen; Joseph meets his father, weeps on his neck, and Israel says he can die now.
kw: The word of God to the patriarchs and the prophets at moments of great decision (15:1; 26:24; Isaiah 41:10). Faith begins where fear is answered by a promise.
The promise first made to Abraham (12:2) is renewed in a place that seems the opposite of promise. Israel will become a people in Egypt, not in Canaan.
to go up, to bring up
God promises that he will “bring you up” again. In the Bible this is the language of the Exodus and of the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. The descent to Egypt already carries the hope of a return.
vv: God spoke to Israel in visions of the night, and said, “Jacob, Jacob.”
God calls by name, twice, as he did to Abraham (22:11) and to Moses (Exodus 3:4). The old man hears the name of his beginning.
do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there.
God does not avoid Egypt; he goes into it. The place of danger becomes the place of growth.
I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again;
Two promises: presence and return. The same God who goes down with Jacob will later go down to see Israel’s affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:7–8).
Joseph’s own hand shall close your eyes.
A tender promise: Jacob will die in the presence of the son he thought dead.
I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive.
Jacob’s words recall Simeon in the Temple, who was ready to depart in peace after seeing the child (Luke 2:29–30). A long grief ends in joy.
ch: The Church reads the descent of Israel into Egypt in the light of the Exodus and of the flight of the Holy Family into Egypt, where Matthew sees Hosea’s words fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). The word of God to Jacob, “I myself will go down with you”, is read as a promise of God’s nearness. The Catechism teaches that the Son of God came down from heaven for us and for our salvation (CCC 456), so that God has gone down to share our condition. When the Church prays for migrants and refugees, this text gives a warm reminder: God does not leave those who are sent into another land.

r.h: Sheep in the midst of wolves
set: The mission discourse now turns from the instructions to the cost. After the details of the journey, Jesus is open with the Twelve: they will meet hostility. Matthew writes for a community, probably Jewish-Christian in origin, that already knew rejection and persecution, and the words of Jesus are placed where his readers could recognize their own experience.

Background. The first disciples were all Jews. When Jesus warns that they will be handed over to councils and flogged in the synagogues (v. 17), he speaks of conflicts inside the Jewish world of the first century, between a Jewish teacher’s followers and other Jewish authorities. This must never be turned into a charge against the Jewish people. The warnings also reach to governors and kings and to the Gentiles (v. 18), and to families (v. 21).
str: v. 16: sheep among wolves; be wise as serpents, innocent as doves.
vv. 17–18: they will be handed over to councils, flogged in synagogues and brought before governors and kings, as a testimony.
vv. 19–20: do not worry about what to say; the Spirit of your Father will speak through you.
vv. 21–23: betrayal even within families; hatred for the sake of Jesus’ name; the one who endures will be saved; flee to the next town.
kw: The word for practical wisdom, the sense of the one who builds his house on rock (7:24). The serpent’s cleverness in the story of Genesis is here turned to good use.

Literally unmixed, as of pure metal or undiluted wine. The disciple is to be simple and without double dealing. Prudence without simplicity becomes cunning; simplicity without prudence becomes naivety.
Not only to put up with, but to remain under: the staying power of those who keep faith under pressure.
vv: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves;
The sender is Jesus, “I am sending you”. The disciples are not sent to be safe but to be faithful, and the Shepherd goes with the sheep.
so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
Both together. Jesus does not call for naivety, and he does not call for cleverness that lies.
do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say;
The promise is not that there will be no trial but that the Spirit will give the word at the hour. It does not forbid preparation for teaching; it speaks of the hour of testimony.
it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
The martyrs have often recalled this. The words of witness are a gift of God, and so the witness is not a matter of eloquence.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Salvation is God’s gift and also asks for perseverance. The Church speaks of final perseverance as a grace that we ask for (CCC 1821).
When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next;
Flight is not cowardice. Jesus himself withdrew when his hour had not yet come, and the Church has never required anyone to seek martyrdom.
ch: The Church sees in this Gospel the pattern of all Christian witness. The Catechism teaches that the disciple must not only keep the faith but profess it and bear witness to it with confidence (CCC 1816), and that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). The last words of v. 23, “before the Son of Man comes”, have been understood in several ways, as referring to the Resurrection and Pentecost, to the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, or to the continuing mission to Israel until the end; the Church does not settle the question by a definition. The Church’s own history confirms the warning: in every century Christians in many lands have been hated for the name of Jesus, and she prays today for all who suffer for the faith, and for those who wrong them.

qa: Does Jesus want his disciples to run away from persecution?

He allows it. “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next” shows that prudence is part of discipleship. The Church honours the martyrs who stood firm when flight was not possible or when faith itself was at stake, but she has never taught that anyone should seek suffering for its own sake.
rite: Today the Roman Calendar gives the optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the 120 martyrs of China canonized in the year 2000, who died between the seventeenth and the twentieth century. Zhao Rong was a soldier who guarded a bishop under arrest, was moved by his witness, became a Christian and later a priest, and died in prison in 1815. Their story shows how Jesus’ words, “the Spirit of your Father speaking through you”, have been lived.
study: Where in my life do I feel “like a sheep among wolves”, and how can I be wise and innocent there at the same time?
Jacob was afraid to leave the promised land, and God said, “I myself will go down with you.” What fear of mine can I put before God in prayer today?
